section.heading: 12.4. The Cross Product
section.paragraph: Given two nonzero vectors, it is very useful to be able to find a nonzero vector that is perpendicular to both of them, as we will see in the next section and in Chapters 13 and 14. We now define an operation, called the cross product, that produces such a vector.
section.heading: The Cross Product of Two Vectors
section.paragraph: Given two nonzero vectors $$\mathbf{a} = {\langle{a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}}\rangle}$$ and $$\mathbf{b} = {\langle{b_{1},b_{2},b_{3}}\rangle}$$ , suppose that a nonzero vector $$\mathbf{c} = {\langle{c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}}\rangle}$$ is perpendicular to both $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ . Then $$\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c} = 0$$ and $$\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c} = 0$$ and so

note.title: Definition of the Cross Product
note.heading: Definition of the Cross Product
note.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{a} = {\langle{a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}}\rangle}$$ and $$\mathbf{b} = {\langle{b_{1},b_{2},b_{3}}\rangle}$$ , then the cross product of $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ is the vector

section.paragraph: Notice that the cross product $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$$ of two vectors $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ , unlike the dot product, is a vector (whereas the dot product is a scalar). For this reason it is also called the vector product. Note that $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$$ is defined only when $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ are three-dimensional vectors.
In order to make Definition 4 easier to remember, we use the notation of determinants. A determinant of order $$2$$ is defined by
$$\left| \begin{array}{lc} a & b \\ c & d \end{array} \right| = ad - bc$$
(Multiply across the diagonals and subtract.) For example,
$$\left| \begin{matrix} 2 & 1 \\ {- 6} & 4 \end{matrix} \right| = 2(4) - 1( - 6) = 14$$
A determinant of order $$3$$ can be defined in terms of second-order determinants:

$$\left| \begin{array}{lcc} a_{1} & {a_{2}} & {a}_{3} \\ b_{1} & b_{2} & b_{3} \\ c_{1} & c_{2} & c_{3} \end{array} \right| = a_{1}\left| \begin{array}{lc} b_{2} & b_{3} \\ c_{2} & c_{3} \end{array} \right| - a_{2}\left| \begin{array}{lc} b_{1} & b_{3} \\ c_{1} & c_{3} \end{array} \right| + a_{3}\left| \begin{array}{lc} b_{1} & b_{2} \\ c_{1} & c_{2} \end{array} \right|$$

Observe that each term on the right side of Equation 5 involves a number $$a_{i}$$ in the first row of the determinant, and $$a_{i}$$ is multiplied by the second-order determinant obtained from the left side by deleting the row and column in which $$a_{i}$$ appears. Notice also the minus sign in the second term. For example,

$$\begin{array}{l} {\left| \begin{matrix} 1 & 2 & {- 1} \\ 3 & 0 & 1 \\ {- 5} & 4 & 2 \end{matrix} \right| = {1\left| \begin{array}{lc} 0 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 \end{array} \right| - 2\left| \begin{matrix} 3 & 1 \\ {- 5} & 2 \end{matrix} \right| + \left( {- 1} \right)\left| \begin{matrix} 3 & 0 \\ {- 5} & 4 \end{matrix} \right|}} \\ {\phantom{\left| \begin{array}{lcc} 1 & 2 & {- 1} \\ 3 & 0 & 1 \\ {- 5} & 4 & 2 \end{array} \right|} = {1(0 - 4) - 2(6 + 5) + ( - 1)(12 - 0) = - 38}} \end{array}$$

If we now rewrite Definition 4 using second-order determinants and the standard basis vectors $$\mathbf{i}$$ , $$\mathbf{j}$$ , and $$\mathbf{k}$$ , we see that the cross product of the vectors $$\mathbf{a} = a_{1}\mathbf{i} + a_{2}\mathbf{j} + a_{3}\mathbf{k}$$ and $$\mathbf{b} = b_{1}\mathbf{i} + b_{2}\mathbf{j} + b_{3}\mathbf{k}$$ is

$$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \left| {\begin{array}{lc} a_{2} & a_{3} \\ b_{2} & b_{3} \end{array}} \middle| \right.\mathbf{i} - \left| {\begin{array}{lc} a_{1} & a_{3} \\ b_{1} & b_{3} \end{array}} \right|\mathbf{j} + \left| {\begin{array}{lc} a_{1} & a_{2} \\ b_{1} & b_{2} \end{array}} \right|\mathbf{k}$$
In view of the similarity between Equations 5 and 6, we often write
$$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \left| \begin{array}{lcc} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ a_{1} & a_{2} & a_{3} \\ b_{1} & b_{2} & b_{3} \end{array} \right|$$

Although the first row of the symbolic determinant in Equation 7 consists of vectors, if we expand it as if it were an ordinary determinant using the rule in Equation 5, we obtain Equation 6. The symbolic formula in Equation 7 is probably the easiest way of remembering and computing cross products.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{a} = {\langle{1,3,4}\rangle}$$ and $$\mathbf{b} = {\langle{2,7, - 5}\rangle}$$ , then

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} = \left| \begin{array}{rrr} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 3 & 4 \\ 2 & 7 & {- 5} \end{array} \right|} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} = {\left| {\begin{array}{rr} 3 & 4 \\ 7 & {- 5} \end{array}} \right|\mathbf{i} - \left| \begin{array}{cr} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & {- 5} \end{array} \right|\mathbf{j} + \left| {\begin{array}{lc} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 7 \end{array}} \right|\mathbf{k}}} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} = {\left( {- 15 - 28} \right){\mathbf{i}} - \left( {- 5 - 8} \right){\mathbf{j}} + \left( {7 - 6} \right){\mathbf{k}} = - 43\mathbf{i} + 13\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}}} \end{array}$$

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Show that $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{a} = 0$$ for any vector $$\mathbf{a}$$ in $$V_{3}$$ .
Solution If $$\mathbf{a} = {\langle{a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}}\rangle}$$ , then

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{a}} = \left| \begin{array}{lcc} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ a_{1} & a_{2} & a_{3} \\ a_{1} & a_{2} & a_{3} \end{array} \right|} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{a}} = {\left( {a_{2}a_{3} - a_{3}a_{2}} \right){\mathbf{i}} - \left( {a_{1}a_{3} - a_{3}a_{1}} \right){\mathbf{j}} + \left( {a_{1}a_{2} - a_{2}a_{1}} \right){\mathbf{k}}}} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{a}} = {0\mathbf{i} - 0\mathbf{j} + 0\mathbf{k} = 0}} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Properties of the Cross Product
section.paragraph: We constructed the cross product $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$$ so that it would be perpendicular to both $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ . This is one of the most important properties of a cross product, so let’s emphasize and verify it in the following theorem and give a formal proof.

note.title: Theorem
note.heading: Theorem
note.paragraph: The vector $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$$ is orthogonal to both $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ .

note.title: Proof
note.heading: Proof
note.paragraph: In order to show that $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$$ is orthogonal to $$\mathbf{a}$$ , we compute their dot product as follows:

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\left( {\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{a}} = {\left| \begin{array}{lc} a_{2} & a_{3} \\ b_{2} & b_{3} \end{array} \right|a_{1} - \left| \begin{array}{lc} a_{1} & a_{3} \\ b_{1} & b_{3} \end{array} \right|a_{2} + \left| \begin{array}{lc} a_{1} & a_{2} \\ b_{1} & b_{2} \end{array} \right|a_{3}}} \\ {\phantom{\left( {\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{a}} = a_{1}\left( a_{2}b_{3} - a_{3}b_{2} \right) - a_{2}\left( a_{1}b_{3} - a_{3}b_{1} \right) + a_{3}\left( a_{1}b_{2} - a_{2}b_{1} \right)} \\ {\phantom{\left( {\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{a}} = {a_{1}a_{2}b_{3} - a_{1}b_{2}a_{3} - a_{1}a_{2}b_{3} + b_{1}a_{2}a_{3} + a_{1}b_{2}a_{3} - b_{1}a_{2}a_{3}}} \\ {\phantom{\left( {\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{a}} = 0} \end{array}$$

A similar computation shows that $$\left( {\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{b} = 0$$ . Therefore $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$$ is orthogonal to both $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ .

section.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ are represented by directed line segments with the same initial point (as in Figure 1), then Theorem 8 says that the cross product $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$$ points in a direction perpendicular to the plane through $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ . It turns out that the direction of $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$$ is given by the right-hand rule: if the fingers of your right hand curl in the direction of a rotation (through an angle less than $$180^{{^\circ}}$$ ) from $$\mathbf{a}$$ to $$\mathbf{b}$$ , then your thumb points in the direction of $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$$ .

image.alt: Details The figure has two parts. In the first part, three vectors are displayed, all three begin from a common point. The first vector, labeled vector a, slopes downward to the left. The second vector, labeled vector b, slopes downward to the right at an angle theta from vector a. The third vector, the labeled cross product of vector a and vector b, rises vertically upward, at right angles to both vectors a and b. The second part of the figure is an illustration of the right hand with its thumb pointing vertically upward, parallel to the cross product of vectors a and b and the fingers of the hand curl in the counterclockwise direction.

figure.caption: The right-hand rule gives the direction of $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$$ .

section.paragraph: Now that we know the direction of the vector $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$$ , the remaining thing we need to complete its geometric description is its length $$\left| {\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} \right|$$ . This is given by the following theorem.

note.title: Theorem
note.heading: Theorem
note.paragraph: If $$\theta$$ is the angle between $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ (so $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \pi$$ ), then the length of the cross product $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$$ is given by

note.paragraph: From the definitions of the cross product and length of a vector, we have

note.heading: Corollary
note.paragraph: Two nonzero vectors $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ are parallel if and only if

note.title: Proof
note.heading: Proof
note.paragraph: Two nonzero vectors $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ are parallel if and only if $$\theta = 0$$ or $$\pi$$ . In either case $$\sin\theta = 0$$ , so $$\left| {\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} \right| = 0$$ and therefore $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = 0$$ .

section.paragraph: Geometric characterization of $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$$

Since a vector is completely determined by its magnitude and direction, we can now say that for nonparallel vectors $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ , $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$$ is the vector that is perpendicular to both $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ , whose orientation is determined by the right-hand rule, and whose length is $$\left| \mathbf{a} \right|\left| \mathbf{b} \right|\sin\theta$$ . In fact, that is exactly how physicists define $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$$ .

The geometric interpretation of Theorem 9 can be seen by looking at Figure 2. If $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ are represented by directed line segments with the same initial point, then they determine a parallelogram with base $$\left| \mathbf{a} \right|$$ , altitude $$\left| \mathbf{b} \right|\sin\theta$$ , and area
$$A = \left| \mathbf{a} \right|\left( {\left| \mathbf{b} \right|\sin\theta} \right) = \left| {\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} \right|$$
Thus we have the following way of interpreting the magnitude of a cross product.

The first vector, labeled vector a, slopes gradually upward to the right and runs along the entire length of the base of the parallelogram. The second vector, labeled vector b, slopes steeply upward to the right and runs along the entire length of the left side of the parallelogram, which is at an angle theta from the base. From the tip of vector b, a dashed line segment, labeled abs(b) sin(theta), is drawn to the base such that it meets the base at right angles to it.

section.paragraph: The length of the cross product $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$$ is equal to the area of the parallelogram determined by $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ .

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find a vector perpendicular to the plane that passes through the points $$P(1,4,6)$$ , $$Q( - 2,5, - 1)$$ , and $$R(1, - 1,1)$$ .

Solution The vector $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PQ}} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PR}}$$ is perpendicular to both $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PQ}}$$ and $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PR}}$$ and is therefore perpendicular to the plane through $$P$$ , $$Q$$ , and $$R$$ . We know from (12.2.1) that

$$\begin{array}{ccl} \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PQ}} & = & {\left( {- 2 - 1} \right)\mathbf{i} + \left( {5 - 4} \right)\mathbf{j} + \left( {- 1 - 6} \right)\mathbf{k} = - 3\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - 7\mathbf{k}} \\ \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PR}} & = & {\left( {1 - 1} \right)\mathbf{i} + \left( {- 1 - 4} \right)\mathbf{j} + \left( {1 - 6} \right)\mathbf{k} = - 5\mathbf{j} - 5\mathbf{k}} \end{array}$$
We compute the cross product of these vectors:

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PQ}} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PR}}} = \left| \begin{array}{rrr} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {- 3} & 1 & {- 7} \\ 0 & {- 5} & {- 5} \end{array} \right|} \\ {\phantom{\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PQ}} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PR}}} = {\left( {- 5 - 35} \right)\mathbf{i} - \left( {15 - 0} \right)\mathbf{j} + \left( {15 - 0} \right)\mathbf{k} = - 40\mathbf{i} - 15\mathbf{j} + 15\mathbf{k}}} \end{array}$$

So the vector $$\langle{- 40, - 15,15}\rangle$$ is perpendicular to the given plane. Any nonzero scalar multiple of this vector, such as $$\langle{- 8, - 3,3}\rangle$$ , is also perpendicular to the plane.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find the area of the triangle with vertices $$P(1,4,6)$$ , $$Q( - 2,5, - 1)$$ , and $$R(1, - 1,1)$$ .

Solution In Example 3 we computed that $$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PQ}} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PR}} = {\langle{- 40, - 15,15}\rangle}$$ . The area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides $$\mathit{PQ}$$ and $$\mathit{PR}$$ is the length of this cross product:
$$|\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PQ}} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{\mathit{PR}}| = \sqrt{{({- 40})}^{2} + {({- 15})}^{2} + 15^{2}} = 5\sqrt{82}$$
The area $$A$$ of the triangle $$PQR$$ is half the area of this parallelogram, that is, $$\frac{5}{2}\sqrt{82}$$ .

section.paragraph: If we apply Theorems 8 and 9 to the standard basis vectors $$\mathbf{i}$$ , $$\mathbf{j}$$ , and $$\mathbf{k}$$ using $$\theta = \pi/2$$ , we obtain

$$\begin{array}{cll} {{\mathbf{i} \times \mathbf{j} = \mathbf{k}} } & {{\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{k} = \mathbf{i}} } & {\mathbf{k} \times \mathbf{i} = \mathbf{j}} \\ {{\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{i} = - \mathbf{k}} } & {{\mathbf{k} \times \mathbf{j} = - \mathbf{i}} } & {\mathbf{i} \times \mathbf{k} = - \mathbf{j}} \end{array}$$
Observe that
$$\mathbf{i} \times \mathbf{j} \neq \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{i}$$
Thus the cross product is not commutative. Also
$$\mathbf{i} \times \left( {\mathbf{i} \times \mathbf{j}} \right) = \mathbf{i} \times \mathbf{k} = - \mathbf{j}$$
whereas
$$\left( {\mathbf{i} \times \mathbf{i}} \right) \times \mathbf{j} = 0 \times \mathbf{j} = 0$$
So the associative law for multiplication does not usually hold; that is, in general,
$$\left( {\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} \right) \times \mathbf{c} \neq \mathbf{a} \times \left( {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right)$$
However, some of the usual laws of algebra do hold for cross products. The following theorem summarizes the properties of vector products.

note.title: Properties of the Cross Product
note.heading: Properties of the Cross Product
note.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{a}$$ , $$\mathbf{b}$$ , and $$\mathbf{c}$$ are vectors and $$c$$ is a scalar, then

section.paragraph: These properties can be proved by writing the vectors in terms of their components and using the definition of a cross product. We give the proof of Property 5 and leave the remaining proofs as exercises.
section.heading: Proof of Property 5
section.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{a} = {\langle{a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}}\rangle}$$ , $$\mathbf{b} = {\langle{b_{1},b_{2},b_{3}}\rangle}$$ , and $$\mathbf{c} = {\langle{c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}}\rangle}$$ , then

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\mathbf{a} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right)} = {a_{1}\left( {b_{2}c_{3} - b_{3}c_{2}} \right) + a_{2}\left( {b_{3}c_{1} - b_{1}c_{3}} \right) + a_{3}\left( {b_{1}c_{2} - b_{2}c_{1}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{a} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right)} = {a_{1}b_{2}c_{3} - a_{1}b_{3}c_{2} + a_{2}b_{3}c_{1} - a_{2}b_{1}c_{3} + a_{3}b_{1}c_{2} - a_{3}b_{2}c_{1}}} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{a} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right)} = {\left( {a_{2}b_{3} - a_{3}b_{2}} \right)c_{1} + \left( {a_{3}b_{1} - a_{1}b_{3}} \right)c_{2} + \left( {a_{1}b_{2} - a_{2}b_{1}} \right)c_{3}}} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{a} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right)} = {\left( {\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{c}}} \end{array}$$
section.heading: Triple Products
section.paragraph: The product $$\mathbf{a} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right)$$ that occurs in Property 5 is called the scalar triple product of the vectors $$\mathbf{a}$$ , $$\mathbf{b}$$ , and $$\mathbf{c}$$ . Notice from Equation 12 that we can write the scalar triple product as a determinant:
$$\mathbf{a} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right) = \left| \begin{array}{lcc} a_{1} & {a_{2}} & {a_{3}} \\ b_{1} & b_{2} & b_{3} \\ c_{1} & c_{2} & c_{3} \end{array} \right|$$

The geometric significance of the scalar triple product can be seen by considering the parallelepiped determined by the vectors $$\mathbf{a}$$ , $$\mathbf{b}$$ , and $$\mathbf{c}$$ . (See Figure 3.) The area of the base parallelogram is $$A = \left| {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right|$$ . If $$\theta$$ is the angle between $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}$$ , then the height $$h$$ of the parallelepiped is $$h = \left| \mathbf{a} \right|\left| {\cos\theta} \right|$$ . (We must use $$\left| {\cos\theta} \right|$$ instead of $$\cos\theta$$ in case $$\theta > \pi/2$$ .) Therefore the volume of the parallelepiped is
Thus we have proved the following formula.

The first vector, labeled vector a, slopes steeply upward to the right and runs along the entire length of the right side of the front face. The second vector, labeled vector b, runs horizontally rightward and along the entire length of the bottom side of the front face. The third vector, labeled vector c, is horizontal and runs along the entire length of the left side of the base. From the top left corner of the front face of the parallelepiped, a dashed line segment extends leftward to meet the vertical vector at a height h from its starting point.

section.paragraph: The volume of the parallelepiped determined by the vectors $$\mathbf{a}$$ , $$\mathbf{b}$$ , and $$\mathbf{c}$$ is the magnitude of their scalar triple product:
$$V = \left| {\mathbf{a} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right)} \right|$$

If we use the formula in (14) and discover that the volume of the parallelepiped determined by $$\mathbf{a}$$ , $$\mathbf{b}$$ , and $$\mathbf{c}$$ is $$0$$ , then the vectors must lie in the same plane; that is, they are coplanar.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Use the scalar triple product to show that the vectors $$\mathbf{a} = {\langle{1,4, - 7}\rangle}$$ , $$\mathbf{b} = {\langle{2, - 1,4}\rangle}$$ , and $$\mathbf{c} = {\langle{0, - 9,18}\rangle}$$ are coplanar.
Solution We use Equation 13 to compute their scalar triple product:

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\mathbf{a} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right)} = \left| \begin{array}{rrr} 1 & 4 & {- 7} \\ 2 & {- 1} & 4 \\ 0 & {- 9} & 18 \end{array} \right|} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{a} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right)} = {1\left| \begin{array}{cr} {- 1} & 4 \\ {- 9} & 18 \end{array} \right| - 4\left| \begin{array}{cr} 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 18 \end{array} \right| - 7\left| \begin{array}{lc} 2 & {- 1} \\ 0 & {- 9} \end{array} \right|}} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{a} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right)} = {1(18) - 4(36) - 7\left( {- 18} \right) = 0}} \end{array}$$

Therefore, by (14), the volume of the parallelepiped determined by $$\mathbf{a}$$ , $$\mathbf{b}$$ , and $$\mathbf{c}$$ is $$0$$ . This means that $$\mathbf{a}$$ , $$\mathbf{b}$$ , and $$\mathbf{c}$$ are coplanar.

section.paragraph: The product $$\mathbf{a} \times \left( {\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}} \right)$$ that occurs in Property 6 is called the vector triple product of $$\mathbf{a}$$ , $$\mathbf{b}$$ , and $$\mathbf{c}$$ . Property 6 will be used to derive Kepler’s First Law of planetary motion in Chapter 13. Its proof is left as Exercise 50.
section.heading: Application: Torque
section.paragraph: The idea of a cross product occurs often in physics. In particular, we consider a force $$\mathbf{F}$$ acting on a rigid body at a point given by a position vector $$\mathbf{r}$$ . (For instance, if we tighten a bolt by applying a force to a wrench as in Figure 4, we produce a turning effect.) The torque $$\mathbf{\tau}$$ (relative to the origin) is defined to be the cross product of the position and force vectors
$$\mathbf{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}$$
and measures the tendency of the body to rotate about the origin. The direction of the torque vector indicates the axis of rotation. According to Theorem 9, the magnitude of the torque vector is
$$\left| \mathbf{\tau} \right| = \left| {\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}} \right| = \left| \mathbf{r} \right|\left| \mathbf{F} \right|\sin\theta$$

where $$\theta$$ is the angle between the position and force vectors. Observe that the only component of $$\mathbf{F}$$ that can cause a rotation is the one perpendicular to $$\mathbf{r}$$ , that is, $$\left| \mathbf{F} \right|\sin\theta$$ . The magnitude of the torque is equal to the area of the parallelogram determined by $$\mathbf{r}$$ and $$\mathbf{F}$$ .

image.alt: Details The figure displays a three dimensional rendering of a bolt, a wrench, and three vectors. The bolt is being tightened by the wrench. A vector labeled, vector tau, begins from the center of the bolt head and runs along the axis of the bolt. Another vector, labeled vector r, begins from the center of the bolt head and runs along the length of the wrench until its tip. The third vector, labeled vector F, begins from the tip of vector r and slopes downward to the right at an angle of theta from vector r.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: A bolt is tightened by applying a $$40$$ -N force to a $$0.25$$ -m wrench, as shown in Figure 5. Find the magnitude of the torque about the center of the bolt.

image.alt: Details The figure displays a three dimensional rendering of a bolt, a wrench, a vector, and a line. The bolt is being tightened by the wrench with the wrench sloping upward to the right. The length of the wrench is 0.25 meters. A dashed line extends upward to the right from the tip of the wrench along the same direction as the wrench. The vector, labeled 40 newton's, begins from the tip of vector r and slopes downward to the right at an angle of 75 degrees from the dashed line.

example.paragraph: Solution The magnitude of the torque vector is

$$\begin{array}{l} {\left| \mathbf{\tau} \right| = \left| {\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}} \right| = \left| \mathbf{r} \right|\left| \mathbf{F} \right|\sin 75^{{^\circ}} = (0.25)(40)\sin 75^{{^\circ}}} \\ {\phantom{\left| \mathbf{\tau} \right|} = {10\sin 75^{{^\circ}} \approx 9.66N \cdot m}} \end{array}$$
If the bolt is right-threaded, then the torque vector itself is
$$\mathbf{\tau} = \left| \mathbf{\tau} \right|\mathbf{n} \approx 9.66\mathbf{n}$$
where $$\mathbf{n}$$ is a unit vector directed down into the page (by the right-hand rule).

section.heading: Discovery Project The Geometry of a Tetrahedron
section.paragraph: A tetrahedron is a solid with four vertices, $$P$$ , $$Q$$ , $$R$$ , and $$S$$ , and four triangular faces, as shown in the figure.

image.alt: Details A three dimensional rendering of a tetrahedron is displayed. The tetrahedron has a horizontal base. The front left vertex of the base is labeled Q. The front right vertex of the base is labeled R. The back vertex of the base is labeled S. The top vertex of the tetrahedron is labeled P.

list.item: Let $$\mathbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{2}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}_{3}$$ , and $$\mathbf{v}_{4}$$ be vectors with lengths equal to the areas of the faces opposite the vertices $$P$$ , $$Q$$ , $$R$$ , and $$S$$ , respectively, and directions perpendicular to the respective faces and pointing outward. Show that $$\mathbf{v}_{1} + \mathbf{v}_{2} + \mathbf{v}_{3} + \mathbf{v}_{4} = 0$$

The volume $$V$$ of a tetrahedron is one-third the distance from a vertex to the opposite face, times the area of that face. Find a formula for the volume of a tetrahedron in terms of the coordinates of its vertices $$P$$ , $$Q$$ , $$R$$ , and $$S$$ . Find the volume of the tetrahedron whose vertices are $$P\left( {1,1,1} \right)$$ , $$Q\left( {1,2,3} \right)$$ , $$R\left( {1,1,2} \right)$$ , and $$S\left( {3, - 1,2} \right)$$ .

Suppose the tetrahedron in the figure has a trirectangular vertex $$S$$ . (This means that the three angles at $$S$$ are all right angles.) Let $$A$$ , $$B$$ , and $$C$$ be the areas of the three faces that meet at $$S$$ , and let $$D$$ be the area of the opposite face $$PQR$$ . Using the result of Problem 1, or otherwise, show that $$D^{2} = A^{2} + B^{2} + C^{2}$$ (This is a three-dimensional version of the Pythagorean Theorem.)

note.title: Hamilton
note.heading: Hamilton
note.paragraph: The cross product was invented by the Irish mathematician Sir William Rowan Hamilton (1805–1865), who had created a precursor of vectors, called quaternions. When he was five years old Hamilton could read Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. At age eight he added French and Italian and at ten he could read Arabic and Sanskrit. At the age of 21, while still an undergraduate at Trinity College in Dublin, Hamilton was appointed Professor of Astronomy at the university and Royal Astronomer of Ireland!
